newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Truth elusive in French economic debate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Truth elusive in French economic debate.

text.p: French businessman Erwan Jestin says he has a serious problem.

"The government is constantly on my back," said Jestin, whose company Broadway and Cie imports micro-brewed American beer."I spend at least half a day a week on paperwork and during that time I'm not out seeing clients,"

It's so bad, Jestin said, that companies -- including his -- are reluctant to hire new workers because they don't generate enough income to pay the social charges the government requires or justify the paperwork involved.
As a result, hiring in France is slow to non-existent, and job creation lags badly compared to economies in the United States, Britain and other parts of the world.

The feeble jobs growth in a faltering economy raise serious questions about the durability of France's traditional interventionist economic management, with its expensive cradle-to-grave welfare system and state control of business.

And little wonder. Alain Juppe, the most unpopular prime minister since the founding of France's Fifth Republic in 1958, presides over an economy with record 12.6 percent unemployment, sickly consumer confidence and weak industrial production.

The economy's fragility stands in stark contrast to the powerful economic performance of the United States and fuels a debate over whether the French-style mixed economy can survive into the 21st century.
LABOUR LAWS, TAXES AND BENEFITS HINDER ECONOMY

Free market politicians, economists and business leaders in France contend that strict labour laws, vertiginous taxes and over-generous social benefits prevent the world's fourth-largest economy from reaching its potential.

Lined up against them is a vocal association of opposition politicians, trade unions and social thinkers who say the managed economy and welfare system are expressions of France's commitment to equality and its determination to stand against what they see as insidious effects of "globalisation".

The conservative government, meanwhile, is frantically in search of a middle way between the European and U.S. systems, combining the flexibility and job creation of the U.S. model with the security and generosity found in continental Europe.
Many doubt the U.S. model of economic flexibility could serve as a panacea for France.
"There is no economic truth, and economics cannot be without links to culture, history and politics," said Rene Valladon, economic secretary of the independent Force Ouvriere union.

As an example of the difference in cultural attitudes, observers cite American acceptance of the business cycle's ups and downs, while French workers expect more stability and see the cycle as an unavoidable evil from which the government should protect them.

European economic systems are at least partly a response to the high unemployment and economic instability that historians say helped push Europe into two world wars, said Paul Horne, international economist with Smith Barney.
"There has been a lot of effort expended creating a comfortable system in Europe because after World War Two they had just been through that ghastly experience," Horne said.
"The United States has not been through that since the Civil War (in the 1860s). If it had, its attitude might be different."
There is widespread agreement on both sides of the Atlantic that the suppleness of the U.S. economy comes at a high price of wage disparity, job insecurity and anxiety.

But most economists and some French government officials say France leans too far in the other direction, providing so much security employers are overburdened with taxes, paperwork and labour laws to hire people.
"France could use a little insecurity," one cabinet minister said privately.
FRANCE MUST ACCEPT SOME CHANGE, EXPERTS SAY

Most economic experts and officials say that, despite widespread resistance, France must accept at least some change to its economic structures if it wants to hold its place near the top of the economic heap.

"There will come a time when we will have to accept that the socio-economic model created after World War Two no longer corresponds to reality," said Herve Goulletquer, economist with France's Banques Populaire.
"If we don't, we will be locked into a cycle of higher and higher unemployment and lower and lower growth."

Data from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) that measure the rate at which posts are created and destroyed and the frequency at which people change jobs show that in France, labour turnover in 1990 was 58 percent of total employment. That is less than half the 126.4 percent in the United States and lower than Germany's or Italy's.

Small business owners face such a mountain of regulations, taxes and other charges that doing business in France has degenerated into a running battle with authorities with barely enough time left for day-to-day company operations, Jestin said.
Entrepreneurs feel victimised by a bureaucracy they say has it in for them and penalises them for doing well.
"The more money you earn, the more often you end up getting audited," Jestin said. "In France, they don't let you make money so people don't work, they just go on vacation."
A spokesman for France's ministry of small businesses said he could not specify how many different taxes the average French business is subjected to.
"Honestly I think you are getting into an area that would take months to unravel," the spokesman told Reuters.

In what could be seen as a measure of the government's weight in the French economy, OECD figures show that in 1995, 48.8 percent of all the money in France was collected by the government and 53.7 percent of spending was government outlays.
This compares with U.S. government receipts of 31.3 percent and outlays of 33.3 percent.
Defenders of the government's high profile point to its successes like high speed TGV trains and France Telecom, France's most profitable company.
But opponents say that for each success, there is at least one setback, like France's failed efforts to build a world-scale computer industry.
Former president Valerie Giscard d'Estaing was recently quoted in the French daily Le Figaro as saying high payroll charges were the main reason for unemployment.
"The (monthly) minimum wage is 6,010 French francs ($1,163) but the employer has to pay 8,410 francs," he said. "There's the main reason for unemployment."
Some economists say the high employment costs freeze in place an insider/outsider dynamic which benefits people with jobs at the expense of job seekers.
Despite mounting evidence that something in the French economy is not working, many defend the system.
"I don't believe this is a real problem because France's cost of labour is about average," said Vadallon.
He said definitions of labour cost differ from country to country and render comparisons difficult. He rejected the criticism that labour laws are too strict in France.
"It's not true anymore. The labour market in France has been deregulated a lot in recent years."
But in the end, culture and history may weigh more than hard data. Workers, politicians and thinkers in France exhibit a visceral reaction to the free-wheeling ways of the U.S. economy.
Jacques Attali, a former senior adviser to socialist President Francois Mitterrand, summed up this response in a recent television appearance.
"I could never accept a society in which insecurity and inequality are the basic assumptions of the system," he said.
($1=5.166 French Franc)
